one_liner: A wide-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 1.8x fair value. Interesting below about $170.

profile.what: Visa runs the largest card-payment network in the world, connecting billions of cards with tens of millions of merchants and thousands of banks.
profile.money: Visa does not lend money. It charges small fees on every payment: service fees on payment volume, data-processing fees per transaction, and higher fees for cross-border payments. Banks issue Visa-branded cards and take the credit risk.
profile.valued: Visa is valued on P/E and free cash flow at a premium for its very high margins and durable growth. Threats to the multiple are regulation of card fees and new payment systems that bypass card networks.

summary.sentence: The largest payment network: very high margins, durable growth and regulatory attention.
strengths: Near-98% gross margin and about 50% net margin.
Asset-light: free cash flow roughly equals earnings.
Long runway in cross-border and emerging markets.
risks: About 35x earnings leaves little margin of safety.
Persistent regulatory and litigation risk on interchange fees.
Debt to assets is fine, but book equity is not growing.

meaning.what_it_does: Runs the world's largest card-payment network, connecting banks, merchants and cardholders.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: A small fee on every transaction that crosses its network, plus cross-border and value-added services. It takes no credit risk.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Cash keeps shifting to digital payments worldwide, and every new card and merchant makes the network more valuable.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Regulation capping fees, or new rails (real-time bank payments, stablecoins, big-tech wallets) routing around the card networks.

moat.summary: A textbook network moat: merchants accept Visa because cardholders carry it, and vice versa. A new entrant cannot break that loop.

industry.summary: Payments innovate constantly, but Visa usually absorbs new methods onto its network.

management.summary: Consistent growth and buybacks that return more than all earnings, so book equity stays flat while per-share value compounds.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $20.9B a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 8–14% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 66%; cost of capital 9.5%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
